portion_doctrine: Segments 11-12 are location-scouting video transcripts covering 100+ LA filming locations across 8 different YouTube videos (Heat, To Live and Die in LA, Atlas Obscura Adventure series, Locationland with Robert Foulkes, E! News coverage, and top 21 LA activities). Core operating principle: precise geo-tagging and photo-matching of real-world filming locations with explicit building identifiers, bridge names, street coordinates, and landmark references. Emphasis on verifiable location pinpointing for film tourism, with practical visitor notes (parking, hours, permissions). Junk content: 40% is UI boilerplate, timestamp sync markers, scene dialogue excerpts, repetitive introductions. Real value is 60%: location names, cross-street coordinates, building identifiers, practical scouting tips, historical context (year filmed, director, actor), and time-indexed visual matching techniques.
operating_rules: Exact address + cross-street reference required (e.g., '9024 Thrasher Avenue in Hollywood Hills', 'intersection of Grand Avenue and 5th Street')
Visual landmark matching: identify buildings in movie shot, match to current real-world location via Google Earth, note architectural changes
Time-indexed proof: footage timestamp ties scene to exact location (e.g., '14:29 building still there')
Permission notation: flag closed-to-public locations (California Edison in Torrance, warehouse with security gate)
Current state annotation: document what's changed since filming ('turned into little league field', 'now renovated senior living community')
Parking and accessibility practical info for location scouts
Multi-location verification: same sequence often shot across 3-7 different locations, piece them together per production requirements
Google Maps/Google Earth is primary verification tool for location scouts
skills: Location matching via visual analysis (building facades, utility poles, landscape features)
Historical research (year filmed, production notes, director decisions)
Change documentation (temporal comparison of location state)
Practical scouting (parking availability, public access, permit requirements)
tools: Google Maps (street view and distance confirmation)
YouTube video timestamps (tie scene to location via frame reference)
gates: Public accessibility: confirm whether location is visitable or closed to public (permission blocks)
Visual match confidence: can current-day Google Earth/street view definitively match movie scene
Architectural integrity: location sufficiently unchanged to be recognizable
prompts: Can you spot [landmark/building] in the background of frame at [time]?
What address matches these visual elements: [building facade], [utility pole], [landscape]?
Compare Google Earth [year] view vs current state: what's changed?
Is this location accessible to public? Parking? Hours?
Which production team photo/shot list documents this specific angle?

weird_gold: Tank #1200002 in shipping yard used as location identifier in Heat (15:27) - ultra-specific visual marker
Circus Liquor neon clown sign predates 1963 signage date: actual 1959 installation, demonstrating verification depth
Brady Bunch house '2 bed 3 bath not 3+3' math reference shows production constraint analysis (why small house chosen despite large onscreen family)
True Lies horse in elevator: protection protocol detail (rubber mats for horse slip prevention) reveals practical location department tactics
Multi-location piecing in single sequence: True Lies 'five locations in two states' for DC lobby scene demonstrates how compositing/editing creates false location continuity
Parking bear at Millennium Biltmore vs free street spot luck factor shows location scout resource variance
Google Maps iconic markers now exist for Terminator 2 bridge (12:13) and Heat locations, validating film-location-to-tourism pipeline
Architectural change documentation methodology: specific notation of 'that building right there' visual matching creates replicable verification pattern
116-year architectural survival: Rosenheim house 1908 to present (5:57 timestamp) validates analog permanence vs set demolition
Bond between location and movie mythology: 'forget it Jake it's Chinatown' (1974) still invoked as #1 LA movie on voting lists, location doctrine as cultural anchor
